page.title: This CEO is out for blood - Fortune

normalized.quote: In the fall of 2003, Elizabeth Holmes, a 19-year-old sophomore at Stanford, plopped herself down in the office of her chemical engineering professor, Channing Robertson, and said, “Let’s start a company.”
normalized.why: This claim specifies the date, name, age, and location of the meeting.

normalized.quote: Now she’s 30, and her private, Palo Alto-based corporation, called Theranos–the name is an amalgam of the words “therapy” and “diagnosis”–has 500 employees and has raised more than $400 million from equity sales to investors who have effectively valued the company at more than $9 billion.
normalized.why: This claim provides checkable numbers for age, employee count, funds raised, and valuation.

normalized.quote: Theranos today is a potentially highly disruptive upstart in America’s $73 billion diagnostic-lab industry, which performs nearly 10 billion tests a year and is estimated to provide the basis for about 70% of doctors’ medical decisions.
normalized.why: This claim includes specific financial and volume statistics for the diagnostic-lab industry.

normalized.quote: Medicare and Medicaid each pay roughly $10 billion annually on reimbursements for these tests.
normalized.why: This claim gives specific annual spending amounts for Medicare and Medicaid.

normalized.quote: It currently offers more than 200–and is ramping up to offer more than 1,000–of the most commonly ordered blood diagnostic tests, all without the need for a syringe.
normalized.why: This claim provides specific test count figures offered by the company.

normalized.quote: Its phlebotomists currently take physician-ordered blood draws (and saliva, urine, feces, and other samples) at collection centers the company operates at its headquarters in Palo Alto and at 21 Walgreens–one in Palo Alto and the rest in Phoenix.
normalized.why: This claim lists specific locations and numbers of Walgreens collection centers.

normalized.quote: Precisely how Theranos accomplishes all these amazing feats is a trade secret.
normalized.why: The text states how the mechanism works is a trade secret, preventing verification.

normalized.quote: Holmes will only say–and this is more than she has ever said before–that her company uses “the same fundamental chemical methods” as existing labs do.
normalized.why: The founder answers how the technology works with a generic statement.

normalized.quote: Holmes counters that because, as noted, her tests employ “the same fundamental chemical methods” as existing tests, peer-review publication of validation studies is both unnecessary and inappropriate.
normalized.why: The speaker gives a generic answer where a specific one was asked for.

facts: Elizabeth Holmes founded Theranos after dropping out of Stanford University in 2003.
Theranos has raised more than $400 million from equity sales, valuing the company at over $9 billion.
The company operates a high-complexity laboratory certified by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
Theranos tests require only a few drops of blood collected via a finger stick into a tiny vial called a nanotainer.
The company's prices are set to never exceed half the Medicare reimbursement rate for each procedure.
Theranos has collection centers at its headquarters in Palo Alto and at 21 Walgreens drugstores.
